Batched inference systems achieve throughput efficiency by grouping requests into a single forward pass, but this design creates a fundamental tension: all sequences in a batch must reach the same length before the compute kernel can terminate, meaning a single 4096-token outlier forces every 128-token request in that batch to pad to 4096 tokens — wasting FLOPS and, critically, holding shorter requests hostage to the outlier's generation time. The central question is not "how fast is my average latency?" but rather "what determines the shape of my P95/P99 latency distribution, and why does tail latency degrade non-linearly as batch size grows?" Experts focus on three interlocking failure modes that beginners ignore: first, padding waste asymmetry — the FLOP cost is symmetric but the delay cost is asymmetric, falling entirely on short requests; second, queue starvation — when a scheduler holds short requests waiting to fill a batch with other short requests, those requests can starve behind a flood of long requests being greedily batched for throughput; third, continuous batching's incomplete fix — iteration-level scheduling (as in vLLM's original design) reduces padding by allowing mid-generation evictions, but reintroduces variance through preemption jitter and KV cache reallocation latency. The beginner sees mean throughput as the optimization target; the expert sees tail latency as a stability property of the scheduling policy, and worries that standard SLO metrics (P50, P95) mask bimodal latency distributions where a subset of request classes — specifically short-context, low-token-count requests — experience disproportionate starvation relative to their computational cost.

Continuous batching eliminates static padding but replaces it with preemption-induced recomputation latency: when a new high-priority request arrives and the KV cache is full, the scheduler must evict one or more in-flight requests, discarding their cached key-value states, and those requests must either wait for cache space and recompute from token 0 (recompute eviction) or have their KV blocks swapped to CPU DRAM (swap eviction). The variance introduced here is structurally different from padding waste — it is conditionally triggered and multiplicative: a request that has already generated 800 tokens and is evicted must pay the full prefill cost again for those 800 tokens, meaning latency variance is now a function of how far along a request was when evicted, not just its total length. vLLM's original PagedAttention design (Kwon et al., 2023) uses a last-in-first-out eviction policy for KV blocks, which is cache-efficient but worst-case for tail latency because recently-admitted long requests that haven't yet built up output tokens get prioritized for eviction, while older long requests with large caches become effectively "too expensive to evict" and crowd out shorter requests. Whether variance is bounded or unbounded depends critically on whether the eviction policy enforces a cap on recomputation debt: systems that allow unbounded recomputation (no limit on how many times a request can be preempted) can produce latency multipliers of 5–20× for unlucky requests in high-load regimes, while policies like Sarathi-Serve's chunked prefill (Agrawal et al., 2023) bound variance by splitting large prefills into fixed-size chunks, preventing any single request from monopolizing the forward pass and thereby stabilizing the preemption trigger rate. The expert worry is that eviction policy and scheduling policy are coupled but often tuned independently — an aggressive admission controller that maximizes batch occupancy will increase eviction frequency, and if the eviction policy doesn't account for per-request recomputation cost (proportional to tokens already generated), tail latency for long-running requests becomes a random walk rather than a predictable function of request length.

In a mixed prefill-decode batch, the forward pass services two computationally distinct phases simultaneously: prefill tokens are compute-bound (high arithmetic intensity, parallelizable across the prompt length) while decode steps are memory-bandwidth-bound (one token per sequence, bottlenecked on KV cache reads). When chunk size is set too small — say 64 or 128 tokens against a decode batch of 128 concurrent sequences — the prefill chunk contributes negligible FLOP density to the forward pass, meaning the GPU's compute units are underutilized while the memory subsystem is already saturated by decode KV fetches; the net effect is that you pay the full kernel launch and scheduling overhead for the prefill chunk without meaningfully amortizing it against useful compute. Sarathi-Serve's own ablations show that chunk sizes below ~512 tokens begin degrading decode throughput on A100s because the prefill FLOP contribution drops below the threshold needed to keep tensor cores occupied during the combined forward pass, effectively making the mixed batch worse than a pure decode batch at the same batch width. The decode-to-prefill ratio matters because it sets the memory pressure baseline: with 128 decoding sequences each requiring KV reads proportional to their context length, the memory bus is nearly saturated before the prefill chunk even executes, so a small chunk adds latency (through kernel fusion overhead) without adding enough compute to justify the cost. The pathological case is a thrashing regime where chunk size is so small that many chunks are required to complete a single prefill, each chunk interrupting a decode step — at 64-token chunks for a 4096-token prompt, you inject 64 decode interruptions per prefill completion, and if each interruption adds even 0.5ms of scheduling overhead, the cumulative prefill latency penalty exceeds what a single uninterrupted prefill would have cost. The correct operating point is chunk size tuned so the prefill FLOP count is roughly iso-latency with one decode step across the current batch width — a moving target that depends on batch size, model width, and context length distribution, which is why systems like DejaVu and later SGLang moved toward adaptive chunk sizing rather than static configuration.

Requests that trigger extended chain-of-thought (CoT) or multi-step tool-call loops are structurally unpredictable at admission time because their output length is not a property of the prompt alone but of the model's intermediate reasoning state — a prompt that looks like a 200-token question may induce 4000 tokens of scratchpad reasoning if the model determines the question requires decomposition, meaning the auxiliary length predictor, trained on (prompt, early decode tokens), will assign these requests a short-output prior that is systematically wrong in a directionally biased way: CoT-triggering requests look like short requests until they aren't, and by the time the scheduler observes the deviation (say, at token 300 when expected output was 150), the request has already been classified as low-growth and over-admission has occurred based on that misclassification. The propagation path is concrete: the scheduler's endogenous growth rate estimate is computed as Σ(predicted_remaining_tokens × per_token_bytes), and underestimating remaining output for 10 CoT requests by 2000 tokens each understates the endogenous KV growth rate by 10 × 2000 × per_token_bytes — on a 70B model with 80-layer KV at bf16, this is roughly 10 × 2000 × 1.6MB ≈ 32GB of unaccounted future KV read volume, causing the scheduler to admit prefill chunks sized as if decode steps will stay fast when they will in fact slow by 2–4× as CoT sequences accumulate length. The failure mode this produces is a soft memory cliff: the scheduler continues admitting new requests because its forward model predicts sufficient headroom, KV cache fills faster than projected, and the system hits one of two bad outcomes — either the KV cache exhausts and forces preemption of partially-completed CoT sequences (which is especially expensive because recomputing 2000 tokens of reasoning context is far costlier than recomputing a short answer), or the system enters a latency inversion where newly admitted short requests are held behind CoT sequences consuming disproportionate memory bandwidth. Tool-call loops compound this because each tool invocation resets the scheduler's output length estimate — the model emits a tool call token, execution happens externally, and the response is appended, making the sequence appear to "restart" with a new short output prediction when it is actually mid-way through a multi-hop reasoning chain that will continue for thousands more tokens. The correct mitigation is online length re-estimation with asymmetric correction: at each decode step, compare actual tokens generated against the predicted output length, and apply an exponential update that weights upward revisions more heavily than downward ones — a Bayesian prior that reflects the empirical skew of CoT length distributions, which have heavy right tails (underestimation is common and large, overestimation is rare and small) as documented in reasoning model evaluations for GPT-o1-class systems where output length variance exceeds mean by factors of 3–8×.
